title: Sulla Marches on Rome
objective: After this level you can explain why Sulla’s march on Rome broke a taboo.
summary: In 88 BCE Sulla led his army against Rome itself, fought Marius’s side in a civil war, then ruled as dictator with no time limit.

cards.headline: In 88 BCE a Roman general did the unthinkable: he attacked Rome.
cards.body: Remember those soldiers who looked to their general, not the Senate? Now see what happens when a general points them at Rome.

cards.headline: The march
cards.body: In 88 BCE Sulla marched his army on Rome itself, something no Roman general had done before. His soldiers followed him, not the Senate: Marius’s reform at work, in the worst possible way. Sulla and Marius, with their supporters, then fought a civil war for control of Rome. The army that was supposed to protect the city was now fighting over it.

cards.headline: Lists of the doomed
cards.body: Sulla won, and took the dictatorship with no time limit. Remember Level 12: a dictator was meant to be an emergency ruler for six months at most. Then came the proscription lists. If your name was on one, you were an enemy who could be killed and your property seized. A public notice that was also a death warrant. Sulla reformed the constitution to strengthen the Senate, and then, surprisingly, retired.
cards.callout: Proscription: a list of enemies who could be killed

cards.headline: Why it mattered
cards.body: Sulla gave up power, but he couldn’t take back what he had shown: an army loyal to its general could be marched on Rome. Before 88 BCE, no Roman general had done it. After 88 BCE, it was no longer unthinkable, just something that had been done before. The first time is the hard part. The next general wouldn’t have to be first.

cards.headline: Sulla: understood
learned: Sulla marched on Rome in 88 BCE
Civil war followed between Sulla and Marius
He ruled as dictator with no time limit

questions.prompt: What did Sulla do in 88 BCE that no general had done before?

options.label: Refused a triumph
options.rationale: His act was far more dangerous.

questions.explanation: Sulla led his legions against Rome itself, breaking a deep taboo.

options.label: New taxes charged on the provinces
Laws banning gladiator shows in Rome
Lists of enemies who could be killed

questions.explanation: Anyone on a proscription list could be killed and have their property seized.

questions.prompt: From Level 12: how did Sulla’s dictatorship break with tradition?

options.label: It was held by two men
It was given by the plebeians
It had to be approved by augurs

questions.explanation: A traditional dictator served at most six months; Sulla took the office with no time limit.
